content: Pelvic organ prolapse (POP) is a condition that affects up to 50% of women who have given birth, with 14% to 19% of these women eventually undergoing surgical correction. Despite the frequency of these surgeries, there is limited evidence in the medical literature regarding the effectiveness of preoperative and postoperative interventions specifically tailored to these procedures. The primary goal of perioperative interventions is to minimize adverse events and improve patient outcomes following surgery for POP. While some interventions, such as the use of prophylactic antibiotics before abdominal surgeries, are well-established, others are unique to POP surgeries and require further investigation. The objective of this review was to evaluate the safety and effectiveness of various perioperative interventions compared to either no intervention or alternative interventions during POP surgery. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving women undergoing surgical treatment for symptomatic POP. The primary outcomes assessed were objective failure of the surgery at any site and subjective postoperative prolapse symptoms. Secondary outcomes included adverse events such as intraoperative blood loss, need for blood transfusion, intraoperative ureteral injury, and postoperative urinary tract infections. A total of 15 RCTs involving 1992 women from five countries were included in the review. These trials assessed eight different perioperative interventions. However, most interventions were evaluated in only one trial, and the quality of evidence ranged from very low to moderate. The main limitation of the studies was imprecision due to small sample sizes and low event rates. Pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT) was one of the interventions studied. Women in the PFMT group attended six perioperative consultations over a three-month period surrounding their surgery. The results showed no clear evidence of a difference in objective surgical failure rates between the PFMT group and the control group at 12 to 24 months post-surgery (odds ratio [OR] 0.93, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.56 to 1.54; moderate-quality evidence). Regarding patients' awareness of prolapse symptoms, the findings were inconsistent. One trial found no difference between groups at 24 months (OR 1.07, 95% CI 0.61 to 1.87; low-quality evidence), while another small trial reported a reduction in symptoms based on a questionnaire completed by the intervention group at 12 months (mean difference [MD] -3.90, 95% CI -6.11 to -1.69; low-quality evidence). Additionally, there were no significant differences in rates of repeat surgery or pessary use for prolapse at 24 months (OR 1.92, 95% CI 0.74 to 5.02; low-quality evidence). Other interventions were evaluated in single RCTs, including preoperative guided imagery, injection of a vasoconstrictor agent at the start of vaginal prolapse surgery, ureteral stent placement during uterosacral ligament suspension, use of a vaginal pack, prophylactic antibiotics for women requiring postoperative urinary catheterization, and postoperative vaginal dilators. Two RCTs assessed bowel preparation, and four RCTs evaluated the method and timing of postoperative catheterization. None of these studies reported the primary outcomes of the review. One study suggested that injecting a vasoconstrictor agent at the start of surgery may reduce intraoperative blood loss by approximately 30 mL. Another study found no clear evidence that ureteral stent placement reduced the risk of intraoperative ureteral injury. Three RCTs examined postoperative urinary tract infections but found no conclusive evidence that the use of a vaginal pack, prophylactic antibiotics, or vaginal dilators influenced infection rates. Other studies did not report on these outcomes. In conclusion, there is a lack of robust data regarding perioperative interventions in POP surgery. A structured program of pelvic floor muscle training before and after surgery did not consistently demonstrate significant benefits, although this conclusion is based on limited evidence from small studies. For other interventions, such as preoperative bowel preparation, vasoconstrictor injection, ureteral stent placement, vaginal pack insertion, vaginal dilators, and prophylactic antibiotics for catheter care, there was no evidence of a reduction in recurrent prolapse rates or clinically meaningful decreases in adverse events, such as intraoperative or postoperative complications. Further high-quality research is needed to better understand the role of these interventions in improving outcomes for women undergoing POP surgery.
